newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: OPEC set to extend current quotas - delegates.
newsitem.headline: OPEC set to extend current quotas - delegates.

text.p: OPEC was set on Wednesday to simply extend current oil output quotas into next year, trusting winter fuel demand will mop up any resumed Iraqi sales and keep prices firm, delegates said.

The Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries seemed to have been lucky as oil ministers checked in to their luxury hotel suites in Vienna ahead of a session of talks about prices and production.
The United Nations looked closer to relaxing its ban on oil exports by Iraq than at any time since it was imposed in 1990, when the Iraqis invaded Kuwait.
OPEC had before it data from industry monitors suggesting violations of mandated quotas had propelled cartel output a million barrels a day above an agreed ceiling.

Yet oil prices are not collapsing. Nobody is raising the threat of imminent glut. The world benchmark Brent Blend of North Sea crude oil ended Tuesday at $22.75 per barrel, up from $18 when OPEC held its last meeting on June 7.
In New York, January crude oil futures rose 13 cents Tuesday to $23.62 a barrel on the New York Mercantile Exchange.

The surprise rally has resulted from unexpectedly low output by non-OPEC sellers and from the delay to resumed Iraqi sales under a U.N. oil-for-food accord, after President Saddam Hussein sent troops to northern Iraq when Kurdish faction fighting erupted in September.

Iraq this week accepted U.N. conditions, but oil firms are already scrambling to fill depleted stocks of heating fuel. Snow in Vienna as delegates from OPEC's 11 member nations gathered for Wednesday's meeting underlined the possibility of a harsh northern winter.
A Gulf source said ministers were therefore "99 percent" certain to retain current quotas at least to June 1997.
The source said OPEC linchpin Saudi Arabia shared the view that demand could absorb the proposed Iraqi sales, of oil worth $2 billion to buy food and medicine.
"The market is very healthy. Demand is strong. Stocks are low. And winter has just started," said the source.
The present quota accord was reached in June and made provision for an extra 800,000 barrels a day of Iraqi exports.

Violations of quotas by Venezuela and others are said by Western monitors to have lifted actual output, even without any Iraqi sales, by almost a million barrels a day above the agreed ceiling of 25.03 million.
The Saudis and Gulf allies Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates feel that, vexing as the violations may be, the market can absorb even more oil.
